In practice

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• fully writable (copy-on-write1)

• dropped at container’s end of life (unless a commit is made)

• a network stack

• with its own private address (by defaut in 172.17.x.x)

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

1several possible methods: overlayfs (default), btrfs, lvm, zfs, aufs

This document provides a detailed overview of Dockerfile instructions used to configure and manage containerized applications. It includes both textual descriptions and tabular data to explain various Dockerfile commands and their purposes. Key instructions covered include:

1. **CMD Command**: Specifies the default command to run inside the container.
2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

The table included in the document highlights specific instructions such as "USER name: group]" and "STOPSIGNAL signal," providing concise descriptions of their functions.

Main topics and concepts discussed include container configuration, command execution, user permissions, environment management, container health monitoring, network configuration, data persistence, and metadata tagging.

This document provides a detailed overview of various Docker commands, focusing on their functionalities and use cases. It includes both textual descriptions and a structured table format for easy reference. The key topics covered include:

1. **Docker Command Functions**:
   - **docker attach**: Connects to a running container, allowing interaction with its standard input, output, and error streams.
   - **docker cp**: Facilitates file transfer between the host and the container. It supports two operations:
     - Copying files from a container to the host.
     - Copying files from the host into a container.
   - **docker export**: Exports the entire content of a container as a tar archive, useful for backups or migrations.
   - **docker exec**: Executes commands within an existing container, often used for debugging purposes.
   - **docker wait**: Pauses execution until a container stops, then returns its exit code.
   - **docker commit**: Creates a new Docker image from a container's current state, effectively capturing a snapshot.

2. **Main Concepts**:
   - Container management and interaction.
   - File transfer between host and container environments.
   - Container lifecycle management, including execution, termination, and state preservation.

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

{"raw_text": "Other security considerations

• images are immutable

→ need a process to apply automatic security upgrades, e.g: • apply upgrades & commit a new image • regenerate the image from the Dockerﬁle

• docker engine control == root on the host machine • give access to the docker socket only to trusted users

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

→ avoid binding subdirectories, prefer using named volumes

2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

In practice

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• fully writable (copy-on-write1)

• dropped at container’s end of life (unless a commit is made)

• a network stack

• with its own private address (by defaut in 172.17.x.x)

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

   - **docker attach**: Connects to a running container, allowing interaction with its standard input, output, and error streams.

This document provides a detailed overview of Dockerfile instructions used to configure and manage containerized applications. It includes both textual descriptions and tabular data to explain various Dockerfile commands and their purposes. Key instructions covered include:

1. **CMD Command**: Specifies the default command to run inside the container.
2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

Title: Validity of the Analytical Writing Measure in GRE

Description: This document discusses the validity of the Analytical Writing (AW) measure in the GRE General Test. It highlights the importance of AW in graduate studies, emphasizing its unique contribution beyond the Verbal and Quantitative measures. The AW consists of two tasks: constructing an argument and critiquing another's argument. The document presents evidence of AW's construct validity, showing strong positive correlations with academic writing samples. It notes a low correlation with the quantitative measure and a moderate correlation with the verbal measure, indicating AW's distinct value. A graph illustrates the relationship between GRE essay scores and course-related writing samples, showing a positive trend.

Key Concepts: Analytical Writing, GRE General Test, construct validity, academic writing, correlation, Verbal and Quantitative measures, graduate studies, writing assessment.

metadata.original_content:
{"raw_text": "Validity of the Analytical Writing Measure

Because the Kuncel et a/. meta-analysis was conducted before the Analytical Writing (AW) measure was introduced into the GRE General Test, it may be useful to include validity information for this measure. The two tasks that comprise the AW are both considered essential in many fields of graduate study. These two tasks are complementary in that the first requires the writer to construct his/her own argument about an issue, and the second requires a critique of someone else's argument by assessing its claims. For virtually all disciplines, AW adds value to the GRE General Test because it provides unique information about test-taker abilities over and above skills measured in the Verbal and Quantitative measures.

Demonstrating the construct validity of the writing measure can be done by showing how AW correlates with other measures it is intended to resemble. As an illustration, AW correlates positively with other samples of academic writing produced by examinees? as shown in the figure below. Examinees in this study were asked to provide two writing samples: one representing their typical written work and one not quite as well written.

This graph shows that there is a strong positive relationship between the GRE essay scores and both of the writing samples from examinees. It should be noted that the AW correlates with these other indicators of writing skill more closely than does the personal statement that many students submit with their applications.*

Furthermore, data indicate that AW has a low correlation (.21) with the quantitative measure and a moderate correlation (.60) with the verbal measure — a finding that is consistent with the structure and intent of those measures.° Thus, AW is providing unique and valuable information beyond the multiple-choice GRE General Test measures.

rrf.content:
In practice

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• fully writable (copy-on-write1)

• dropped at container’s end of life (unless a commit is made)

• a network stack

• with its own private address (by defaut in 172.17.x.x)

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

1several possible methods: overlayfs (default), btrfs, lvm, zfs, aufs

Results of the Kuncel et al. study

Results from this study show that:

1. The GRE General Test is a “generalizably valid predictor of first-year graduate GPA, overall graduate GPA, comprehensive exam scores, publication citation counts and faculty ratings.”

2. The GRE General Test also correlates positively with degree attainment and research productivity.

3. The GRE General Test has better predictive validity than undergraduate grades or letters of recommendation.

4. The GRE Subject Tests are better predictors of success than either the GRE General Test or undergraduate GPA.

This meta-analysis study is important because these results apply across a range of intended academic majors, across native speakers of English and nonnative speakers of English, across traditional and nontraditional students and across master’s and doctoral programs.”

1 Kuncel, N. R, Hezlett, S. A. and Ones, D. S. (2001). A comprehensive meta-analysis of the predictive validity of the Graduate Record Examinations: \mplications for graduate student selection and performance. Psychological Bulletin, 127 (1), 162-181.

2 The master’s analyses can be found in “The Validity of the Graduate Record Examination for Master's and Doctoral Programs: A Meta-Analytic Investigation” by Kuncel, N.R., Wee, S., Serafin, S. and Hezlett, S.A. (In press) GRE Research Report. Princeton, NJ: ETS.

This document provides a detailed overview of various Docker commands, focusing on their functionalities and use cases. It includes both textual descriptions and a structured table format for easy reference. The key topics covered include:

1. **Docker Command Functions**:
   - **docker attach**: Connects to a running container, allowing interaction with its standard input, output, and error streams.
   - **docker cp**: Facilitates file transfer between the host and the container. It supports two operations:
     - Copying files from a container to the host.
     - Copying files from the host into a container.
   - **docker export**: Exports the entire content of a container as a tar archive, useful for backups or migrations.
   - **docker exec**: Executes commands within an existing container, often used for debugging purposes.
   - **docker wait**: Pauses execution until a container stops, then returns its exit code.
   - **docker commit**: Creates a new Docker image from a container's current state, effectively capturing a snapshot.

Security strategies

Docker containers are not really sandboxed from the host machine. They talk with the same kernel. You may want to consider strategies to reduce the risks of privilege escalation.

Container/Host isolation

• run the container with an ordinary user (docker run -u) • reduce root privileges (capabilities, seccomp, apparmor) • conﬁgure a user namespace

Container/Container isolation

This document provides a detailed overview of Dockerfile instructions used to configure and manage containerized applications. It includes both textual descriptions and tabular data to explain various Dockerfile commands and their purposes. Key instructions covered include:

1. **CMD Command**: Specifies the default command to run inside the container.
2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

The table included in the document highlights specific instructions such as "USER name: group]" and "STOPSIGNAL signal," providing concise descriptions of their functions.

vector.content:
**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

metadata.original_content:
{"raw_text": "Other security considerations

• images are immutable

→ need a process to apply automatic security upgrades, e.g: • apply upgrades & commit a new image • regenerate the image from the Dockerﬁle

• docker engine control == root on the host machine • give access to the docker socket only to trusted users

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

→ avoid binding subdirectories, prefer using named volumes

This document provides a detailed overview of Dockerfile instructions used to configure and manage containerized applications. It includes both textual descriptions and tabular data to explain various Dockerfile commands and their purposes. Key instructions covered include:

1. **CMD Command**: Specifies the default command to run inside the container.
2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

• images are immutable

→ need a process to apply automatic security upgrades, e.g: • apply upgrades & commit a new image • regenerate the image from the Dockerﬁle

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

metadata.original_content:
{"raw_text": "Validity of the Analytical Writing Measure

Because the Kuncel et a/. meta-analysis was conducted before the Analytical Writing (AW) measure was introduced into the GRE General Test, it may be useful to include validity information for this measure. The two tasks that comprise the AW are both considered essential in many fields of graduate study. These two tasks are complementary in that the first requires the writer to construct his/her own argument about an issue, and the second requires a critique of someone else's argument by assessing its claims. For virtually all disciplines, AW adds value to the GRE General Test because it provides unique information about test-taker abilities over and above skills measured in the Verbal and Quantitative measures.

Demonstrating the construct validity of the writing measure can be done by showing how AW correlates with other measures it is intended to resemble. As an illustration, AW correlates positively with other samples of academic writing produced by examinees? as shown in the figure below. Examinees in this study were asked to provide two writing samples: one representing their typical written work and one not quite as well written.

This graph shows that there is a strong positive relationship between the GRE essay scores and both of the writing samples from examinees. It should be noted that the AW correlates with these other indicators of writing skill more closely than does the personal statement that many students submit with their applications.*

Furthermore, data indicate that AW has a low correlation (.21) with the quantitative measure and a moderate correlation (.60) with the verbal measure — a finding that is consistent with the structure and intent of those measures.° Thus, AW is providing unique and valuable information beyond the multiple-choice GRE General Test measures.

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

This document provides a detailed overview of Dockerfile instructions used to configure and manage containerized applications. It includes both textual descriptions and tabular data to explain various Dockerfile commands and their purposes. Key instructions covered include:

1. **CMD Command**: Specifies the default command to run inside the container.
2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

The table included in the document highlights specific instructions such as "USER name: group]" and "STOPSIGNAL signal," providing concise descriptions of their functions.

   - **docker attach**: Connects to a running container, allowing interaction with its standard input, output, and error streams.

   - **docker export**: Exports the entire content of a container as a tar archive, useful for backups or migrations.
   - **docker exec**: Executes commands within an existing container, often used for debugging purposes.
   - **docker wait**: Pauses execution until a container stops, then returns its exit code.
   - **docker commit**: Creates a new Docker image from a container's current state, effectively capturing a snapshot.

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

metadata.original_content:
{"raw_text": "Other security considerations

• images are immutable

→ need a process to apply automatic security upgrades, e.g: • apply upgrades & commit a new image • regenerate the image from the Dockerﬁle

• docker engine control == root on the host machine • give access to the docker socket only to trusted users

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

→ avoid binding subdirectories, prefer using named volumes

In practice

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• fully writable (copy-on-write1)

• dropped at container’s end of life (unless a commit is made)

• a network stack

• with its own private address (by defaut in 172.17.x.x)

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

1several possible methods: overlayfs (default), btrfs, lvm, zfs, aufs

8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

1. **CMD Command**: Specifies the default command to run inside the container.
2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

cohere_reranked.content:
In practice

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• fully writable (copy-on-write1)

8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

A docker container is

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

Title: Validity of the Analytical Writing Measure in GRE

Description: This document discusses the validity of the Analytical Writing (AW) measure in the GRE General Test. It highlights the importance of AW in graduate studies, emphasizing its unique contribution beyond the Verbal and Quantitative measures. The AW consists of two tasks: constructing an argument and critiquing another's argument. The document presents evidence of AW's construct validity, showing strong positive correlations with academic writing samples. It notes a low correlation with the quantitative measure and a moderate correlation with the verbal measure, indicating AW's distinct value. A graph illustrates the relationship between GRE essay scores and course-related writing samples, showing a positive trend.

{"raw_text": "Validity of the Analytical Writing Measure

Because the Kuncel et a/. meta-analysis was conducted before the Analytical Writing (AW) measure was introduced into the GRE General Test, it may be useful to include validity information for this measure. The two tasks that comprise the AW are both considered essential in many fields of graduate study. These two tasks are complementary in that the first requires the writer to construct his/her own argument about an issue, and the second requires a critique of someone else's argument by assessing its claims. For virtually all disciplines, AW adds value to the GRE General Test because it provides unique information about test-taker abilities over and above skills measured in the Verbal and Quantitative measures.

Demonstrating the construct validity of the writing measure can be done by showing how AW correlates with other measures it is intended to resemble. As an illustration, AW correlates positively with other samples of academic writing produced by examinees? as shown in the figure below. Examinees in this study were asked to provide two writing samples: one representing their typical written work and one not quite as well written.

This graph shows that there is a strong positive relationship between the GRE essay scores and both of the writing samples from examinees. It should be noted that the AW correlates with these other indicators of writing skill more closely than does the personal statement that many students submit with their applications.*

Furthermore, data indicate that AW has a low correlation (.21) with the quantitative measure and a moderate correlation (.60) with the verbal measure — a finding that is consistent with the structure and intent of those measures.° Thus, AW is providing unique and valuable information beyond the multiple-choice GRE General Test measures.

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

{"raw_text": "Other security considerations

• images are immutable

→ need a process to apply automatic security upgrades, e.g: • apply upgrades & commit a new image • regenerate the image from the Dockerﬁle

• docker engine control == root on the host machine • give access to the docker socket only to trusted users

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

→ avoid binding subdirectories, prefer using named volumes

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

• images are immutable

→ need a process to apply automatic security upgrades, e.g: • apply upgrades & commit a new image • regenerate the image from the Dockerﬁle

• docker engine control == root on the host machine • give access to the docker socket only to trusted users

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

→ avoid binding subdirectories, prefer using named volumes

2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.

9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.

Multi-stage build (since v17.05)

#======= Stage 1: build the app from sources =======#

FROM debian:stretch AS builder

# update the package lists an install the build dependencies

RUN apt-get -qqy update

RUN apt-get -qqy install gcc make libacme-dev

# install the sources in /opt/src and build them

COPY . /opt/src

RUN cd /opt/src && ./configure && make

# install the ﬁles in a tmp dir and make an archive that we can deploy elsewhere

RUN cd /opt/src && make install DESTDIR=/tmp/dst \

&& cd /tmp/dst && tar czvf /tmp/myapp.tgz .

#======= Stage 2: ﬁnal image ================#

FROM debian:stretch

# update the package lists and install the runtime dependencies

RUN apt-get -qqy update

RUN apt-get -qqy install libacme1.0

# install the app built in stage 1

COPY --from=builder /tmp/myapp.tgz /tmp/

RUN cd / && tar zxf /tmp/myapp.tgz

CMD ["myapp"]

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• a network stack

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.

6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

In practice

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• fully writable (copy-on-write1)

• dropped at container’s end of life (unless a commit is made)

• a network stack

• with its own private address (by defaut in 172.17.x.x)

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

1several possible methods: overlayfs (default), btrfs, lvm, zfs, aufs

This document provides a detailed overview of various Docker commands, focusing on their functionalities and use cases. It includes both textual descriptions and a structured table format for easy reference. The key topics covered include:

1. **Docker Command Functions**:
   - **docker attach**: Connects to a running container, allowing interaction with its standard input, output, and error streams.
   - **docker cp**: Facilitates file transfer between the host and the container. It supports two operations:
     - Copying files from a container to the host.
     - Copying files from the host into a container.
   - **docker export**: Exports the entire content of a container as a tar archive, useful for backups or migrations.
   - **docker exec**: Executes commands within an existing container, often used for debugging purposes.
   - **docker wait**: Pauses execution until a container stops, then returns its exit code.
   - **docker commit**: Creates a new Docker image from a container's current state, effectively capturing a snapshot.

2. **Main Concepts**:
   - Container management and interaction.
   - File transfer between host and container environments.
   - Container lifecycle management, including execution, termination, and state preservation.

   - How can I interact with a running Docker container?
   - What is the method to copy files to and from a Docker container?
   - How do I export a Docker container's content?
   - What command allows running additional processes in a Docker container?

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

This document provides a detailed overview of Dockerfile instructions used to configure and manage containerized applications. It includes both textual descriptions and tabular data to explain various Dockerfile commands and their purposes. Key instructions covered include:

1. **CMD Command**: Specifies the default command to run inside the container.
2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

metadata.original_content:
{"raw_text": "Other security considerations

• images are immutable

→ need a process to apply automatic security upgrades, e.g: • apply upgrades & commit a new image • regenerate the image from the Dockerﬁle

• docker engine control == root on the host machine • give access to the docker socket only to trusted users

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

→ avoid binding subdirectories, prefer using named volumes

Security strategies

Docker containers are not really sandboxed from the host machine. They talk with the same kernel. You may want to consider strategies to reduce the risks of privilege escalation.

Container/Host isolation

• run the container with an ordinary user (docker run -u) • reduce root privileges (capabilities, seccomp, apparmor) • conﬁgure a user namespace

• run the docker engine inside a VM

Container/Container isolation

• disable intercontainer communications (--icc=false) • isolate containers in diﬀerent networks

In practice

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• fully writable (copy-on-write1)

• dropped at container’s end of life (unless a commit is made)

• a network stack

• with its own private address (by defaut in 172.17.x.x)

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

since docker v1.10 but not enabled by default

• UIDs/GIDs inside the containers mapped to another range outside the container

• isolating docker users from each other (one docker daemon for each user, with uids remapped to diﬀerent ranges)

• limits (as of v1.10)

• global conﬁg only (daemon scope) • coarse mapping only (hardcoded range: 0..65535)

User namespaces

since docker v1.10 but not enabled by default

• UIDs/GIDs inside the containers mapped to another range outside the container

• useful for:

• preventing fs-based attacks (eg: root user inside the container creates a setuid executable in an external volume)

• isolating docker users from each other (one docker daemon for each user, with uids remapped to diﬀerent ranges)

• limits (as of v1.10)

• global conﬁg only (daemon scope) • coarse mapping only (hardcoded range: 0..65535)

This document provides a detailed overview of Dockerfile instructions used to configure and manage containerized applications. It includes both textual descriptions and tabular data to explain various Dockerfile commands and their purposes. Key instructions covered include:

1. **CMD Command**: Specifies the default command to run inside the container.
2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

In practice

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• fully writable (copy-on-write1)

• dropped at container’s end of life (unless a commit is made)

• a network stack

• with its own private address (by defaut in 172.17.x.x)

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

This document provides a detailed overview of various Docker commands, focusing on their functionalities and use cases. It includes both textual descriptions and a structured table format for easy reference. The key topics covered include:

1. **Docker Command Functions**:
   - **docker attach**: Connects to a running container, allowing interaction with its standard input, output, and error streams.
   - **docker cp**: Facilitates file transfer between the host and the container. It supports two operations:
     - Copying files from a container to the host.

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

metadata.original_content:
{"raw_text": "Other security considerations

• images are immutable

→ need a process to apply automatic security upgrades, e.g: • apply upgrades & commit a new image • regenerate the image from the Dockerﬁle

• docker engine control == root on the host machine • give access to the docker socket only to trusted users

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

→ avoid binding subdirectories, prefer using named volumes

&& cd /tmp/dst && tar czvf /tmp/myapp.tgz .

RUN apt-get -qqy install libacme1.0

# install the app built in stage 1

COPY --from=builder /tmp/myapp.tgz /tmp/

RUN cd / && tar zxf /tmp/myapp.tgz

This document provides a detailed overview of various Docker commands, focusing on their functionalities and use cases. It includes both textual descriptions and a structured table format for easy reference. The key topics covered include:

1. **Docker Command Functions**:
   - **docker attach**: Connects to a running container, allowing interaction with its standard input, output, and error streams.
   - **docker cp**: Facilitates file transfer between the host and the container. It supports two operations:
     - Copying files from a container to the host.
     - Copying files from the host into a container.
   - **docker export**: Exports the entire content of a container as a tar archive, useful for backups or migrations.
   - **docker exec**: Executes commands within an existing container, often used for debugging purposes.
   - **docker wait**: Pauses execution until a container stops, then returns its exit code.
   - **docker commit**: Creates a new Docker image from a container's current state, effectively capturing a snapshot.

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

This document provides a detailed overview of Dockerfile instructions used to configure and manage containerized applications. It includes both textual descriptions and tabular data to explain various Dockerfile commands and their purposes. Key instructions covered include:

1. **CMD Command**: Specifies the default command to run inside the container.
2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.

8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

This document provides an overview of Docker Machine and Docker Swarm. Docker Machine is described as an abstraction for provisioning and using Docker hosts across local VMs, public cloud, and private cloud environments. The document includes a diagram illustrating the command `$ machine create` and its application in different environments.

Docker Swarm is discussed as a tool for managing a cluster of Docker hosts. It highlights the confusion around the name "swarm," which refers to two different products: the legacy Docker Swarm and a standalone server solution. The legacy Swarm, first released in December 2014, is a superset of the Docker Engine API and requires an external discovery service like etcd or consul. It is network-agnostic, requiring separate configuration of overlay networks.

The document also mentions sections on Docker's introduction, containers, I/O images, builder, security, ecosystem, and future developments. Illustrations include a diagram of Docker Machine environments and an image of Docker containers represented as whales.

It explains how containers are isolated and not directly accessible from outside the network unless port redirection is configured. The document includes instructions on using the `docker run -p [ipaddr:]hostport:containerport` command to redirect incoming connections from a host's TCP port to a container's TCP port.    - **ADD src dst**: Similar to COPY, but with the added capability to automatically extract tar archives and accept HTTP URLs as sources.

It includes key commands and their functionalities, which are essential for users managing Docker containers. The document is structured around a table that lists commands, their syntax, and descriptions of their functions.

   - **`docker ps -a`**: Lists all containers, including those that are stopped.
   - **`docker logs [ -f ] container`**: Displays the output (stdout and stderr) of a specified container, with an option to follow the output in real-time.

This document provides a detailed overview of various Docker commands, focusing on their functionalities and use cases. It includes both textual descriptions and a structured table format for easy reference. The key topics covered include:

1. **Docker Command Functions**:
   - **docker attach**: Connects to a running container, allowing interaction with its standard input, output, and error streams.
   - **docker cp**: Facilitates file transfer between the host and the container. It supports two operations:
     - Copying files from a container to the host.
     - Copying files from the host into a container.
   - **docker export**: Exports the entire content of a container as a tar archive, useful for backups or migrations.
   - **docker exec**: Executes commands within an existing container, often used for debugging purposes.
   - **docker wait**: Pauses execution until a container stops, then returns its exit code.
   - **docker commit**: Creates a new Docker image from a container's current state, effectively capturing a snapshot.

2. **Main Concepts**:
   - Container management and interaction.
   - File transfer between host and container environments.
   - Container lifecycle management, including execution, termination, and state preservation.

1. **CMD Command**: Specifies the default command to run inside the container.
2. **ENTRYPOINT Command**: Defines the command that will always run when the container starts.
3. **USER name[:group]**: Indicates the user and optionally the group under which the command will run. This is crucial for setting permissions and security contexts.
4. **WORKDIR Path**: Sets the working directory inside the container where commands will be executed.
5. **ENV name="value"**: Allows setting environment variables that can be used by applications within the container.
6. **STOPSIGNAL Signal**: Specifies a signal to be sent to the container to terminate it, offering an alternative to the default SIGTERM.
7. **HEALTHCHECK CMD Command**: Provides a command to test the health of the container, ensuring it operates correctly.
8. **EXPOSE Port**: Lists the TCP/UDP ports that the container listens on, facilitating network communication.
9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.
10. **LABEL name="value"**: Used for adding arbitrary metadata to the container, useful for organization and management.

1. **Key Facts and Data Points:**
   - The document outlines several Docker commands used for container management, including creating, starting, stopping, killing, restarting, pausing, unpausing, renaming, updating, and removing containers.

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

• images are immutable

→ need a process to apply automatic security upgrades, e.g: • apply upgrades & commit a new image • regenerate the image from the Dockerﬁle

• docker engine control == root on the host machine • give access to the docker socket only to trusted users

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

9. **VOLUME Path**: Defines mount points for external volumes, enabling persistent data storage.

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• dropped at container’s end of life (unless a commit is made)

• a network stack

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

In practice

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• fully writable (copy-on-write1)

• dropped at container’s end of life (unless a commit is made)

• a network stack

• with its own private address (by defaut in 172.17.x.x)

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

1several possible methods: overlayfs (default), btrfs, lvm, zfs, aufs

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

• images are immutable

• avoid docker run --privileged (gives full root access)

• beware of symlinks in external volumes

eg. ctr1 binds /data, ctr2 binds /data/subdir, if both are malicious and cooperate, ctr1 replaces /data/subdirwith a symlink to /, then on restart ctr2 has access to the whole host ﬁlesystem

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.

A docker image is an immutable snapshot of the ﬁlesystem

A docker container is

• a temporary ﬁle system

• layered over an immutable fs (docker image)

• fully writable (copy-on-write1)

• dropped at container’s end of life (unless a commit is made)

• a network stack

• with its own private address (by defaut in 172.17.x.x)

• a process group

• one main process launched inside the container • all sub-processes SIGKILLed when the main process exits

**Document Description for Content Retrieval:**

Title: Security Considerations in Docker Environments

Section: Part 7 - Security

Summary:
This section discusses various security considerations when working with Docker containers. Key points include:

- **Image Immutability**: Images are immutable, necessitating a process for automatic security upgrades. This involves applying upgrades, committing new images, and regenerating images from Dockerfiles.
  
- **Docker Engine Control**: The Docker engine control equates to root access on the host machine. It is crucial to restrict access to the Docker socket to trusted users only.

- **Avoiding Privileged Mode**: Running containers with `--privileged` grants full root access, which should be avoided to maintain security.

- **Symlink Vulnerabilities**: Caution is advised with symlinks in external volumes. An example scenario is provided where malicious containers could exploit symlinks to gain access to the host filesystem. The recommendation is to avoid binding subdirectories and to use named volumes instead.

Page: 72/84

Keywords: Docker security, image immutability, root access, privileged mode, symlink vulnerabilities, named volumes.
